The Effect of Pre‑Exercise Hyperhydration on Exercise Performance,
Physiological Outcomes and Gastrointestinal Symptoms: A Systematic
Review
William T. Jardine1 · Brad Aisbett1 · Monica K. Kelly1 · Louise M. Burke2 · Megan L. Ross2 ·
Dominique Condo1 · Julien D. Périard3 · Amelia J. Carr1

Accepted: 19 June 2023
© The Author(s) 2023


Abstract
Background Fluid loss during prolonged exercise in hot conditions poses thermoregulatory and cardiovascular challenges
for athletes that can lead to impaired performance. Pre-exercise hyperhydration using nutritional aids is a strategy that may
prevent or delay the adverse effects of dehydration and attenuate the impact of heat stress on exercise performance.
Objectives The aim of this systematic review was to examine the current literature to determine the effect of pre-exercise
hyperhydration on performance, key physiological responses and gastrointestinal symptoms.
Methods English language, full-text articles that compared the intervention with a baseline or placebo condition were
included. An electronic search of Medline Complete, SPORTDiscus and Embase were used to identify articles with the
final search conducted on 11 October 2022. Studies were assessed using the American Dietetic Association Quality Criteria
Checklist.
Results Thirty-eight studies involving 403 participants (n = 361 males) were included in this review (n = 22 assessed exer-
cise performance or capacity). Two studies reported an improvement in time-trial performance (range 5.7–11.4%), three
studies reported an improvement in total work completed (kJ) (range 4–5%) and five studies reported an increase in exercise
capacity (range 14.3–26.2%). During constant work rate exercise, nine studies observed a reduced mean heart rate (range
3–11 beats ­min−1), and eight studies reported a reduced mean core temperature (range 0.1–0.8 °C). Ten studies reported
an increase in plasma volume (range 3.5–12.6%) compared with a control. Gastrointestinal symptoms were reported in 26
studies, with differences in severity potentially associated with factors within the ingestion protocol of each study (e.g. treat-
ment, dose, ingestion rate).
Conclusions Pre-exercise hyperhydration may improve exercise capacity during constant work rate exercise due to a reduced
heart rate and core temperature, stemming from an acute increase in plasma volume. The combination of different osmotic
aids (e.g. glycerol and sodium) may enhance fluid retention and this area should continue to be explored. Future research
should utilise valid and reliable methods of assessing gastrointestinal symptoms. Furthermore, studies should investigate
the effect of hyperhydration on different exercise modalities whilst implementing a strong level of blinding. Finally, females
are vastly underrepresented, and this remains a key area of interest in this area.

Abstract
Background Fluid loss during prolonged exercise in hot conditions poses thermoregulatory and cardiovascular challenges
for athletes that can lead to impaired performance. Pre-exercise hyperhydration using nutritional aids is a strategy that may
prevent or delay the adverse effects of dehydration and attenuate the impact of heat stress on exercise performance.
Objectives The aim of this systematic review was to examine the current literature to determine the effect of pre-exercise
hyperhydration on performance, key physiological responses and gastrointestinal symptoms.
Methods English language, full-text articles that compared the intervention with a baseline or placebo condition were
included. An electronic search of Medline Complete, SPORTDiscus and Embase were used to identify articles with the
final search conducted on 11 October 2022. Studies were assessed using the American Dietetic Association Quality Criteria
Checklist.
Results Thirty-eight studies involving 403 participants (n = 361 males) were included in this review (n = 22 assessed exer-
cise performance or capacity). Two studies reported an improvement in time-trial performance (range 5.7–11.4%), three
studies reported an improvement in total work completed (kJ) (range 4–5%) and five studies reported an increase in exercise
capacity (range 14.3–26.2%). During constant work rate exercise, nine studies observed a reduced mean heart rate (range
3–11 beats ­min−1), and eight studies reported a reduced mean core temperature (range 0.1–0.8 °C). Ten studies reported
an increase in plasma volume (range 3.5–12.6%) compared with a control. Gastrointestinal symptoms were reported in 26
studies, with differences in severity potentially associated with factors within the ingestion protocol of each study (e.g. treat-
ment, dose, ingestion rate).
Conclusions Pre-exercise hyperhydration may improve exercise capacity during constant work rate exercise due to a reduced
heart rate and core temperature, stemming from an acute increase in plasma volume. The combination of different osmotic
aids (e.g. glycerol and sodium) may enhance fluid retention and this area should continue to be explored. Future research
should utilise valid and reliable methods of assessing gastrointestinal symptoms. Furthermore, studies should investigate
the effect of hyperhydration on different exercise modalities whilst implementing a strong level of blinding. Finally, females
are vastly underrepresented, and this remains a key area of interest in this area.

and endurance.


 Methods
 All players who were listed on the NFL’s COVID-19 Injury Reserve (COVID-IR) list were screened for
 inclusion. Players were included in the study if they had spent ≥10 days on the COVID-19 IR list (which
 indicated a positive PCR test based on the NFL COVID-19 policies), had played in at least two games before
 and after going on the IR list, and primarily played an offensive or defensive position. The mean number of
 snaps played per game and Pro Football Focus (PFF) score per game were collected for each athlete, which
 served as surrogate measures of endurance and performance, respectively. The results were analyzed with
 players grouped by position, and then all players grouped as a whole. Within-group comparisons were
 performed via t-tests.


 Results
 A total of 78 players met the criteria for inclusion in the study. The overall mean PFF score pre-COVID-19
 infection was 62.15 (SD: 6.93), while it was 61.73 (SD: 7.42) post-COVID-19 infection, showing a decrease of
 0.42 after infection (n=78, p=0.33). The mean number of snaps played per game pre-COVID-19 infection was
 38.99 (SD: 16.46) while it was 38.10 (SD: 17.05) post-COVID-19 infection, showing a decrease of 0.89 after
 infection (n=78, p=0.30). When grouped by position, statistically significant differences were seen with
 Defensive Backs’ mean snaps played per game decreasing by 18.30 (n=6, p=0.03) and Defensive Linemen’s
 mean PFF score decreasing by 3.77 points (n=21, p=0.03).


 Conclusion
 Based on our findings, COVID-19 infection negatively impacted endurance in Defensive Backs, and
 performance in Defensive Linemen. However, there was inconclusive evidence to show whether COVID-19
 infection negatively impacted other positions when analyzed separately or all positions when analyzed
 together. Further studies with more participants are needed to fully assess the effects of COVID-19 on
 performance and endurance in elite athletes.

{
 "id":"Q68",
 "sourceFile":"The effect of probable COVID-19 infection on the National Football League players performance and endurance during the 2020 season.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in the text, 'The Effect of Probable COVID-19 Infection on the National Football League Players' Performance and Endurance During the 2020 Season', matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Performance","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["American Football"],
 "populations":["Professional / Elite"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Retrospective single-arm cohort of 78 NFL players who spent at least 10 days on the COVID-19 Injury Reserve list in the 2020 season and played in at least two games before and after. Mean Pro Football Focus score was 62.15 before and 61.73 after infection (p = 0.33), and mean snaps per game was 38.99 before and 38.10 after (p = 0.30). Position-level declines were significant only for defensive backs in snaps (n = 6, down 18.30, p = 0.03) and defensive linemen in PFF score (n = 21, down 3.77, p = 0.03).",
 "screeningLimitations":"This is a small, uncontrolled before-and-after comparison, and the position groups are very small (six defensive backs). PFF score and snap count are proxies for performance and endurance, and the design cannot separate infection effects from injuries, rest or other season changes.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the defensive back snap decline as evidence that COVID-19 impairs endurance, when that subgroup has six players and the authors judge the evidence inconclusive overall.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2023,
   "citation":"Walker CR, Belisario J, Abramoff B. The Effect of Probable COVID-19 Infection on the National Football League Players' Performance and Endurance During the 2020 Season. Cureus. 2023;15(3):e35821.",
   "doi":"10.7759/cureus.35821",
   "abstract":"The authors asked whether NFL players with probable COVID-19 in the 2020 season showed a drop in performance or endurance. Players who spent at least 10 days on the league's COVID-19 Injury Reserve list and had played in two or more games before and after were compared using snaps per game and PFF score per game. Across all players, neither measure changed significantly, but defensive backs and defensive linemen showed declines.",
   "tldr":"Among 78 NFL players with probable COVID-19 in 2020, overall performance grades and snap counts did not change significantly after infection. Declines in two small position groups need confirmation in larger samples.",
   "methods":"Retrospective single-arm cohort. Players were drawn from the NFL COVID-19 Injury Reserve list (at least 10 days, two or more games either side of listing, offensive or defensive position). Snaps per game and PFF score per game were compared before and after infection with within-group t-tests, overall and by position.",
   "findings":"PFF score fell from 62.15 to 61.73 (decrease 0.42, p = 0.33) and snaps per game fell from 38.99 to 38.10 (decrease 0.89, p = 0.30) across 78 players. Defensive backs (n = 6) lost 18.30 snaps per game (p = 0.03) and defensive linemen (n = 21) lost 3.77 PFF points (p = 0.03). The authors judge the evidence inconclusive for other positions and for all players combined.",
   "limitations":"Confounders such as injuries to the player or teammates, trades, weekly game strategy, opponent difficulty and officiating were not analysed. Position groups were small, and infection status was inferred from injury-reserve listing rather than medical records, so symptomatic and asymptomatic cases could not be separated. The study also could not distinguish infection effects from extra rest before return.",
   "practicalImplications":"Across the group, performance and snap counts did not change clearly after probable COVID-19. The defensive back and defensive lineman signals suggest staff should track snap counts and performance grades after a player returns from infection, and treat these results as hypotheses to test.",
   "athleteDev":"For performance staff, the study supports monitoring snap counts and performance grades after a player returns from COVID-19, with particular attention to defensive backs and linemen. It does not show that all players lose output.",
   "rtp":"The study does not address medical clearance or safe timing for return to play after COVID-19. It measured in-season output only and cannot set return criteria."
 }
}

{
 "id":"Q69",
 "sourceFile":"The effect of variations in knee and hip angles on electromyographic activity of the hamstrings and related muscles during the Nordic hamstring exercise.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in the text, 'The Effect of Variations in Knee and Hip Angles on Electromyographic Activity of the Hamstrings and Related Muscles During the Nordic Hamstring Exercise', matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"medium",
 "studyDesign":"Laboratory / Experimental Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Rehabilitation","Performance"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Crossover laboratory study of 13 recreationally active male volunteers who performed 5-second isometric Nordic hamstring contractions on a platform inclined at 30 degrees, with knee angles of 30, 50 and 60 degrees and hip angles of 0, 30 and 45 degrees, while surface EMG was recorded. At a hip angle of 0 degrees, biceps femoris, semitendinosus and semimembranosus activity was higher at a knee angle of 30 degrees than at 50 or 60 degrees (p < 0.05). Semimembranosus activity at knee 60 and hip 45 was higher than at knee 60 and hip 0 (p < 0.05).",
 "screeningLimitations":"The sample was 13 recreationally active men rather than athletes, the contractions were isometric, and the board was inclined at only one angle (30 degrees). The study measures muscle activation only, so it cannot show effects on strength, hamstring injury or return to sport.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the higher EMG at a 30-degree knee angle as proof that this position builds more hamstring strength or prevents injury, when the study measured only isometric muscle activation in recreational men.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2024,
   "citation":"Keerasomboon T, Soga T, Hirose N. The Effect of Variations in Knee and Hip Angles on Electromyographic Activity of the Hamstrings and Related Muscles During the Nordic Hamstring Exercise. Int J Sports Phys Ther. 2024;19(3):275-283.",
   "doi":"10.26603/001c.92745",
   "abstract":"The Nordic hamstring exercise is often performed on an inclined board, but isometric hamstring activation across different knee and hip angles has not been well described. The authors measured surface EMG of the hamstrings and related muscles during 5-second isometric Nordic contractions in 13 male volunteers, with knee angles of 30, 50 and 60 degrees and hip angles of 0, 30 and 45 degrees, on a platform inclined at 30 degrees. A knee angle of 30 degrees with hip 0 produced higher activity in three hamstring muscles than knee 50 or 60 degrees.",
   "tldr":"In 13 recreationally active men, isometric Nordic holds with the knee at 30 degrees and the hip at 0 degrees gave higher EMG in three hamstring muscles than knee angles of 50 or 60 degrees. This is an activation result, not a strength or injury result.",
   "methods":"Crossover study. Thirteen male volunteers performed isometric Nordic hamstring contractions on a 30-degree inclined platform at three knee angles (30, 50, 60 degrees) and three hip angles (0, 30, 45 degrees). Knee and hip angles were monitored with an electrical goniometer, and normalised EMG was compared with repeated-measures MANOVA and pairwise tests.",
   "findings":"At a hip angle of 0 degrees, biceps femoris, semitendinosus and semimembranosus EMG was significantly higher at a knee angle of 30 degrees than at 50 or 60 degrees (p < 0.05). Semimembranosus EMG at knee 60 and hip 45 was higher than at knee 60 and hip 0 (p < 0.05). The authors conclude that knee flexion of 30 degrees with hip flexion of 0 degrees gave the most hamstring activation in this set-up.",
   "limitations":"The study had 13 participants, and the authors note the sample was small. The board was inclined only at 30 degrees, which limits generalisation to other board angles or to dynamic Nordic exercise. The study measured isometric EMG only and did not test strength or injury outcomes.",
   "practicalImplications":"When coaches use isometric Nordic holds, a 30-degree knee angle with the hip at 0 degrees produced more hamstring EMG than 50 or 60 degrees in this group of recreational men. Trial the angle with your own athletes before changing programmes, and do not treat EMG as a direct strength or injury measure.",
   "athleteDev":"For strength staff, the study supports treating knee angle as a variable in isometric Nordic work, with 30 degrees and hip 0 giving higher hamstring activation in this sample. Whether this builds strength or reduces injury risk has not been tested.",
   "rtp":"Not directly applicable to return to sport. The participants were uninjured recreational men and the study measured activation only, so it cannot set loads or angles for a rehabilitation or return-to-play plan."
 }
}

 "evidenceSummary":"Randomised, counterbalanced crossover trial in 10 male amateur soccer players completing 60 minutes of a soccer-specific protocol with a 15-minute half-time break. The control was a passive break, and the re-warm-up condition was a passive 12-minute break followed by a 3-minute re-warm-up. The re-warm-up was followed by better 20 m sprint time (3.32 vs 3.42 s, d = 0.6), squat jump height (30.17 vs 26.96 cm, d = 0.6) and countermovement jump height (31.53 vs 28.15 cm, d = 0.7) early in the second half, while perceived exertion was about 2 units higher.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Ten amateur players completed a single soccer-specific protocol rather than match play, so the findings are short-term and small-sample. The effects were acute, and the study did not examine the physiological mechanisms behind them.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the acute sprint and jump gains as a proven match-day advantage, when the trial measured short-term effects in ten amateur players in a simulated protocol.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2020,
   "citation":"Fashioni E, Langley B, Page RM. The effectiveness of a practical half-time re-warm-up strategy on performance and the physical response to soccer-specific activity. J Sports Sci. 2020;38(2):140-149.",
   "doi":"10.1080/02640414.2019.1686941",
   "abstract":"The authors compared a half-time re-warm-up with a passive half-time break in 10 male soccer players completing a 60-minute soccer-specific protocol. The re-warm-up improved 20 m sprint time, squat jump and countermovement jump after the re-warm-up and early in the second half, with no significant change in 5 m or 10 m sprint, muscle soreness or PlayerLoad. Ratings of perceived exertion were higher after the re-warm-up.",
   "tldr":"A 3-minute re-warm-up during a 15-minute half-time break improved 20 m sprint and jump performance early in the second half in amateur players. It also raised perceived exertion, and the effects were short-term.",
   "methods":"Randomised, counterbalanced crossover trial with 10 male amateur soccer players. Each completed 4 x 15-minute periods of a soccer-specific protocol with a 15-minute half-time, either passive (control) or passive 12 minutes plus a 3-minute re-warm-up. Sprint, squat jump, countermovement jump, perceived exertion, muscle soreness and PlayerLoad were measured.",
   "findings":"After the re-warm-up and early in the second half, 20 m sprint time was faster (3.32 vs 3.42 s; d = 0.6), squat jump height was greater (30.17 vs 26.96 cm; d = 0.6) and countermovement jump height was greater (31.53 vs 28.15 cm; d = 0.7). Perceived exertion was about 2 units higher after the re-warm-up. No significant changes were found for 5 m or 10 m sprint, muscle soreness or PlayerLoad.",
   "limitations":"Only 10 amateur male players were studied, and the protocol simulated soccer activity rather than match play. The authors identify a limit on transferring the results to matches and say the mechanisms behind the responses were not considered.",
   "practicalImplications":"A short active re-warm-up during half time may restore some sprint and jump performance in the early second half without raising soreness or PlayerLoad. Coaches should weigh this against the higher perceived exertion it adds, and trial the routine with their own squad before adopting it.",
   "athleteDev":"For performance staff, the study supports trialling a short active re-warm-up at half time, expecting small acute gains in 20 m sprint and jump performance in the first minutes of the second half. Confirm the effect in your own players before making it routine.",
   "rtp":"Not applicable to return to sport. The participants were healthy amateur players and the outcomes were acute performance measures only."
 }
}

 "decision":"INCLUDE",

 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in the text, 'The effectiveness of cryostimulation exposure on sleep and recovery in male athletes: Timing considerations', matches the filename.",

 "studyDesign":"Randomized Controlled Trial",
 "primaryDomain":"Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains":["Recovery & Readiness","Athlete Wellbeing"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Athletic Training","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Endurance Sport"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes","Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Randomised controlled crossover trial of 22 well-trained male athletes or triathletes, each completing a running session and one night of sleep monitoring under three conditions: whole-body cryostimulation (WBC) straight after training at 19:00, WBC one hour before bed at 22:00, or control, one week apart. WBC after training did not change subjective or objective sleep measures compared with control. It did improve cardiac parasympathetic activity, which was greatest the night after the 22:00 exposure, when core body temperature one hour after bedtime was also lowest.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Only men were included, one night was measured per condition, and the sample is small, so the findings may not transfer to women or to longer exposure periods. The sleep result is null, so the positive findings rest on autonomic and temperature measures rather than sleep quality itself.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the autonomic and temperature changes as proof that cryostimulation improves sleep, when the sleep measures themselves did not change after training exposure.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2024,
   "citation":"Arc-Chagnaud C, Dugué B, Bouzigon R, Pla R, Bosquet L, Dupuy O. The effectiveness of cryostimulation exposure on sleep and recovery in male athletes: Timing considerations. Eur J Sport Sci. 2024:1-10.",
   "doi":"10.1002/ejsc.12200",
   "abstract":"The study aimed to test whether whole-body cryostimulation after training improves sleep and recovery, and which timing is best: immediately after training or one hour before bed. Twenty-two well-trained male athletes or triathletes completed three randomised crossover sessions. WBC after training did not change subjective or objective sleep, but it improved cardiac parasympathetic activity, which was most evident after the exposure one hour before bed, where core body temperature was also lowest.",
   "tldr":"In trained male endurance athletes, cryostimulation straight after evening training did not change sleep measures. Exposure one hour before bed gave the clearest overnight autonomic and core temperature changes, but sleep quality itself was unchanged.",
   "methods":"Randomised controlled crossover protocol in 22 well-trained male athletes or triathletes. Each completed a running training session and one night of sleep analysis under WBC at 19:00 (after training), WBC at 22:00 (one hour before bed), or control, with sessions spaced seven days apart. Sleep was measured by actimetry, EEG, heart rate variability, core body temperature and perceptual scales.",
   "findings":"WBC after training did not change subjective or objective sleep parameters compared with control. WBC improved cardiac parasympathetic activity, which was greater overnight after the 22:00 exposure than after the other conditions. Core body temperature one hour after bedtime was lowest in the 22:00 condition. The authors also report a condition effect on slow-wave sleep and a decrease in muscle soreness at the 19:00 time point.",
   "limitations":"Only male participants were included, and the authors note that responses in women may differ and that the menstrual cycle was not considered. Each condition was measured over a single night. The sample was small and well-trained, which limits extrapolation to other populations.",
   "practicalImplications":"Cryostimulation straight after evening training did not change sleep in this group, so it should not be marketed as a sleep aid. Using it about one hour before bed may give better overnight autonomic recovery and a larger core temperature drop than exposure straight after training, and staff can test that timing with their own athletes.",
   "athleteDev":"For performance staff, the study supports trialling whole-body cryostimulation about one hour before bed, rather than straight after an evening session, as a recovery aid for trained male endurance athletes. Track autonomic and temperature responses, because sleep quality itself did not improve.",
   "rtp":"Not applicable to return to sport. The participants were healthy, well-trained athletes, and the study cannot show whether cryostimulation helps recovery after injury or during rehabilitation."
 }
}

 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the running back result as proof that high-stakes games raise concussion risk for backs, when the paper reports it as a small-sample signal that needs confirmation.",

   "doi":"10.7759/cureus.6252",
   "abstract":"Concussion incidence in the NFL generally rises across the season but stagnates or falls in the final quarter. The authors compared concussion incidence in games where at least one team was still in the playoff hunt with games where both teams were eliminated or had clinched, using 166 concussions from weeks 13-16 of the 2012-2015 seasons. Incidence did not differ between the two game types, and plays per game was the main predictor. Running backs showed a higher incidence in hunt games.",
   "tldr":"In NFL weeks 13-16, games with playoff stakes did not have more concussions than games without stakes overall. Running backs were the one position with a higher rate in playoff-hunt games, but the counts are small.",
   "methods":"Concussions from weeks 13-16 of the 2012-2015 NFL regular seasons were taken from PBS Frontline Concussion Watch and matched to 256 games. Each game was classed by playoff status of the teams (in the hunt, clinched or eliminated) and compared using Welch-corrected ANOVA and t-tests. A multivariate regression tested the hunt effect alongside plays per game, altitude, temperature and dew point.",
   "findings":"Concussion incidence was 0.651 per game in hunt games and 0.623 per game in non-hunt games (p = 0.890). Running backs had higher incidence in hunt games (0.049 versus 0.00, p = 0.004), and tight ends showed a similar but non-significant trend. In the regression, game importance was not significant (p = 0.794), while total plays was (beta = 0.01605, p = 0.025).",
   "limitations":"Sample sizes are low in many game-type groups, which produced unequal variances. Week 17 was excluded because teams did not have to report concussions that week, so the data cover less than 50% of non-hunt games.    "practicalImplications":"Playoff stakes alone did not change overall concussion rates in this sample, so staff should not assume that high-stakes games carry more concussion risk for all players.    "athleteDev":"For professional football staff, the practical signal is that total plays per game tracked concussion incidence more closely than game importance. Use this to inform game-load planning rather than assuming that competitive stakes drive injury risk.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot inform return-to-play decisions for an individual player. It describes incidence across games and says nothing about recovery time or clearance after a concussion."
 }
